newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Cyberspace copyright treaties cleared for adoption.
newsitem.headline: Cyberspace copyright treaties cleared for adoption.

text.p: Artists and performers like Madonna will be entitled to get paid when their work is used on the Internet under the first global pacts on copyright in cyberspace due for approval at a U.N. conference Friday.
Senior officials and participants said the last major disputes over who owns what in the tangled world of the Internet were solved in the early hours of Friday.

"We've proved there's dynamism in this community," Jukka Liedes, the Finnish chairman of the talks, said at a conference centre where 800 delegates from 160 nations have been negotiating the pacts since Dec. 2.

Liedes said two treaties on literary and artistic works and on rights of performers and producers of music had been cleared for adoption later in the day while a third one on database producers -- considered dead from the start -- had been shelved.

When ratified by governments, the treaties will create a ground-breaking international agreement to protect digitally transmitted sound recordings and the rights of their performers on the information superhighway.

This means performers such as Madonna, for instance, would be able to use the Internet to distribute her music, have copyrights for it for the first time in the digital era and get paid for it, according to Liedes.
"Madonna will now have the possibility for the first time to make her works available on the Internet and have her rights respected in the digital environment," he told reporters.
The $40-billion-a-year music industry says digital transmission of recordings could represent a $2 billion market.
Liedes said the last major hurdle over the most controversial article in the treaties concerning rights to reproduce material was cleared after the conference agreed to delete it.

That was a victory for online and Internet companies furious that the article would have made even innocent Web surfing, which by definition requires that a computer make transient copies, a copyright violation.
The Internet community, saying the article would expose companies to multibillion-dollar liability and give sweeping powers to copyright-based industries, wanted it deleted altogether.
U.S. Assistant Secretary of Commerce Bruce Lehman proposed deleting the article on Thursday and there was general consensus, a member of the U.S. delegation said.
An official of the Ad Hoc Coalition Group, a broad lobbying group representing online giants and telecommunications companies, welcomed the decision.
"So far so good," said Peter Harter of the Information Technology Association of America, a trade association. "We've done a lot of good here for the Internet. We're reasonably pleased."
Once passed, the treaties will have to be approved by national legislatures, a process that will take some time.
Lehman was due to give a final news conference, followed by one given by European officials.
